Microsoft no longer needs OpenAI to compete at the frontier.

The company just revealed an 8-trillion-parameter base model — built entirely in-house with zero distillation from external models. It uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 80 billion active parameters, and according to Microsoft's Kevin Sullivan, it already outperforms the base model behind GPT 5.6 Soul.

This is a structural shift in the AI industry's power dynamics. For three years, Microsoft bankrolled OpenAI while lacking its own frontier model capability. That dependency is ending. When your largest cloud provider also becomes a direct model competitor, every enterprise AI contract gets re-evaluated.

For CTOs, the immediate question is vendor strategy. If Microsoft embeds this model across Azure, Copilot, and its enterprise stack, the switching costs for organizations locked into Microsoft infrastructure become enormous — but so does the leverage if you are already there.

For CEOs, the deeper signal is that the AI model layer is consolidating around four or five companies with the capital and compute to train at this scale. The window for smaller players to compete on foundation models is closing. The differentiation moves to orchestration, domain specialization, and deployment speed.
